title: Coverage of Private Parking Code of Practice

content.content: Today we laid the new Private Parking Code of Practice before Parliament. This landmark reform will give drivers new rights to challenge unfair private parking charges.

There has been widespread coverage across national media. This includes articles in The Sun, The Guardian, BBC News Online, the Standard, i News, The Times, The Independent, The Telegraph and the Daily Star, which all covered the new Code's guarantee of 5 minutes for drivers to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave once a session ends. Outlets also covered the plans to scrap charges on appeal for situations outside a driver’s control like vehicle breakdowns and medical emergencies,  and the £20 cap on appeal for small slip ups like forgetting a permit or typing in the wrong vehicle registration. Several outlets note this follows a record 16.9 million parking tickets issued last year.

On the morning round, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, Angela Rayner was asked about the announcement and spoke about the benefits of the Code to Times Radio, Sky News Breakfast, BBC Breakfast, LBC, BBC Radio 4’s Today, Good Morning Britain, ITN and Bauer. Additional broadcast coverage featured on outlets including BBC Manchester, Greatest Hits Liverpool & North West, Hits Radio Teeside.

And there was further coverage seen in Auto Express,  Buckinghamshire Live, Eastern Daily Press, Regit, Highways Magazine, The Herts Advertiser, West Bridgford Wire, Oxford Mail, Manchester Evening News, Liverpool Echo, Scotsman, AOL and Fleet News.
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said:

“Parking should be straightforward, not another everyday hassle. These changes mean drivers get a fairer deal, protected time to park and leave without fear of being unfairly charged, and confidence that private parking providers are held to a higher standard.
“It’s yet another step forward in this government’s plan to take the stress out of everyday life and ease the pressure on people’s pockets.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:
“Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them.
“We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off.”

title: Why I brought Europe's infrastructure and nature network to Bristol

content.content: By Louise McGowan, Principal Adviser for Nature-based Solutions and Climate Change, Natural England, and Conference Chair, IENE 2026

The Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe came to the UK for the first time this September, marking its 30th anniversary. Louise McGowan reflects on bringing the conference to Bristol, lessons from colleagues in more than 40 countries, and why nature must be regarded as infrastructure.

In September, the Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe (IENE) came to the UK for the first time, marking 30 years of bringing transport and nature together. Nearly 300 delegates from more than 40 countries spent 5 days in Bristol exploring how we build infrastructure that works for both people and nature. For many UK delegates, it was their first encounter with a community they didn't know existed.
"What an incredible community. I'd never heard of it before."
A delegate said to me halfway through the week, and others told me much the same. For me, this was validation that bringing IENE to the UK had been worth all the effort.
A community worth bringing home
I attended my first IENE conference in Prague in 2024. I'll be honest: when I saw the programme ran for 5 days, I was surprised. By the end of the week, I completely understood why.

IENE brings together people working where infrastructure meets nature, from across Europe and beyond. Ecologists rarely find themselves in the same room as transport planners, engineers, economists, policymakers and infrastructure operators, yet all of them shape the landscapes we depend on. Surrounded by this international community, the field feels large and established. But back home in your day job, it can feel like a very small niche.

I wanted UK colleagues to experience what I experienced in Prague, the realisation that a huge amount of knowledge and practical experience already exists. Across Europe, people are testing solutions, learning from what doesn't work and sharing those lessons. We don't always need another pilot project. Sometimes we simply need to learn from the people who have already done the work.

That diversity of experience showed from the start. Our opening panel in Bristol, Green is Cheaper than Grey, led by Natural England's Oliver Harmar, brought developers, architects, government agencies and industry leaders together to challenge the idea that nature is an added cost. Building nature in from the outset can cut long-term costs, improve resilience and add wider social and environmental value. As panellist Louise Clarke from Berkeley Group said afterwards: "It was refreshing being on a panel and looking out and only recognising one face."

That kind of joined-up conversation is exactly what Natural England's strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, calls for. It recognises that resilient economies, healthy communities and critical infrastructure all depend on functioning natural systems, and that nature recovery can't be delivered in isolation. Bringing IENE to Bristol was a chance to learn from international experience and strengthen the partnerships we need.
Why "the value of nature"?

We deliberately chose the IENE 2026 theme to provoke debate. Some people hear The Value of Nature in Resilient Infrastructure and think of the services nature provides: trees cooling cities, wetlands reducing flood risk, healthy ecosystems helping infrastructure withstand a changing climate. Others think about economics. How do we account for nature in decisions without reducing it to a simple number, and make investment choices that respect ecological limits?

Those questions ran through the week, explored in-depth by Erik Gómez-Baggethun, a leading figure in ecological economics and environmental governance during his keynote. There wasn't a single answer, but there was broad agreement that infrastructure, climate resilience and nature recovery can no longer be treated as separate conversations.
Nature is infrastructure

One of the strongest messages to emerge from the conference was the growing recognition that nature is critical infrastructure. Across the programme, speakers explored how healthy natural systems increase the resilience of transport networks and help deliver better outcomes for people and places.
Reflecting on the discussions, Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, said:

"One thing that came out loud and clear is how nature is infrastructure. Healthy blanket bogs are flood defences and sources of pure water, nature protects infrastructure, including roads and railways that would otherwise flood, and infrastructure can be built more quickly when nature is fully blended into construction plans, such as green bridges over trunk roads. The idea that nature and infrastructure are opposites is an idea well past its sell by date."

That theme came up repeatedly. Speakers from across Europe, South America and beyond showed how green bridges, wildlife crossings, railway corridors and restored habitats are reconnecting fragmented landscapes. Long-term monitoring showed that well-designed crossings improve safety for both wildlife and people. When connectivity is designed in from the start, the benefits go far beyond just for biodiversity's sake.
What we heard from the experts

A keynote that stayed with me came from Manuela Panzacchi of the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research. Her modelling tools show how infrastructure, climate change and other human activity affect wildlife movement, and can test future scenarios to identify the most vulnerable corridors. Whether the discussion was roads, rail, power, ports or urban development, the same principles kept emerging: connectivity matters, ecological limits matter, and nature must be considered from the start.

The policy session was equally thought-provoking. One talk on nature-positive procurement challenged us to build biodiversity into the business case much earlier, before designs are fixed and opportunities are lost.

Another explored liability for wildlife-vehicle collisions across Europe, sparking a fascinating discussion with a colleague from National Highways. We reflected on the UK's limited roadkill data and how lessons from our European counterparts could help us understand the issue better and inform future action.

Technology was another recurring theme, from AI-powered biodiversity monitoring and habitat mapping to collision prediction tools. It's no substitute for ecological expertise, but it is becoming a powerful tool for better-informed decisions.
Seeing Bristol through new eyes
On the Wednesday, delegates joined field trips across the West of England. I joined the Bristol Harbour boat trip and, despite living and working here, learned a huge amount about my own city.

From the water, we passed SS Great Britain and Temple Meads, we saw floating ecosystems and waterfront regeneration transforming former industrial landscapes while protecting the green and blue spaces that make Bristol unique. It was a fitting illustration of the week's central message: with the right planning and ambition, nature and development can reinforce one another.
Leaving a living legacy

The Organising Committee didn't want the conference to disappear as soon as everyone boarded their trains and flights home. Throughout the week, native trees supplied by The Tree Council were displayed across the venue. They are now being planted during National Tree Week as part of the emerging Western Forest, helping create Pucklechurch Wood. Together, they will form the IENE 2026 Copps.
I love the symbolism. For 30 years, IENE has been growing knowledge and partnerships across Europe, and now a small part of that story will literally keep growing in the landscape.
Thirty years on, what next?

The conference closed with reflections from Edgar van der Grift, one of IENE's founding members. From the first IENE conference welcoming less than 100 people from 20 countries to nearly 300 delegates from more than 40 countries in Bristol. Edgar observed that, after 30 years, the ecological viability of IENE itself appeared to be in very healthy condition.
I couldn't agree more. New leadership, a renewed board and a new generation of members bring challenges, but also opportunities. What hasn't changed is the need for the work.

Bristol wasn't a conclusion. It was the next step in putting nature and people at the heart of infrastructure thinking. For Natural England, that's why hosting IENE 2026 mattered. If we're serious about recovering nature for growth, health and security, learning from one another and working beyond traditional boundaries will be essential.
Get involved
If your work or interests sit where infrastructure, transport and nature meet, IENE is a fantastic community to be part of. Find out more at iene.info.

description: The Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe came to the UK for the first time this September, marking its 30th anniversary. Louise McGowan reflects on bringing the conference to Bristol, lessons from colleagues in more than 40 countries, and why nature must be regarded as infrastructure.

title: Want to automate your work? Start with a data spring clean

content.content: My role as the editor of this blog is to find stories, structure them and make sure they are read by people who can benefit. It is an engagement role, not a technical one.
But I am tech-curious. I have worked in tech and data roles in the past and seen first-hand how thoughtful data structures and automation can make workflows quicker and more reliable.
Getting a blog post from idea to publication involved a surprising amount of admin. For our small team, doing much of this manually meant less time to spend developing and sharing brilliant stories.
We spent most of our time looking for information

I’ve used automation tools before and I know the first thing you need is well organised data to build automations on. Data isn’t just the figures we use to evaluate our work. It also includes the documents, emails and deadlines we work with every day
Our information was spread over several locations and applications. For example:

The information was scattered across our systems making it difficult to answer simple questions like “who has approved this blog post?” and “where should we be sharing that blog post?”. It was hard to gauge the blog’s success because all we could easily see was how many people viewed the post, but not how they acted on it.
In short, we were spending a lot of time tracking down information, that we could have spent sharing brilliant stories.
This is not a problem unique to publishing. Many teams manage processes through a mixture of documents, inboxes, task boards and unwritten knowledge.
The tidy up

The first step of the reorganisation was to create a single Source of Truth for the blog. We created a Sharepoint List that would quietly house all available information about blog posts, showing just a neat, useful subset to us as a status board. Each item on the list was linked to a draft document, a group of authors and stakeholders, and a senior approver.

At a glance, we could see where every blog post was in the publishing process, who was writing and reviewing it, and whether it had been approved. Linking list items to draft documents saved us searching through document folders for files named after titles that might be changed and authors that might hand over to others.
Bringing this information together freed up time that was once spent looking for things. However I wanted to go a few steps further.
A little more automation, a little more action
Power Automate is a tool that allows even mildly tech-curious folks like me to build powerful automations without using a single line of code.
Once I had my all-important Single Source of Truth, I had a reliable foundation on which to build automations.

For example, when a card is moved from the “Draft” status column to “Senior Approver Review”, a Power Automate flow looks up who the reviewer should be, grants them access to the linked draft document and sends them an approval message. All the reviewer has to do after reading the draft is add some comments and select “Approved” or “Rejected” in the email. For our team this is a much quicker process than manually granting access and composing an email. It also removes ambiguity from the response.
Every time I celebrate a new automation win, I get asked by colleagues, “How do you know where to start?”

My response is: every time I repeat a task, copy information from one system to another, chase someone, or remind myself what should happen next in a sequence, I have found an opportunity to automate.
I start by writing the process down and identifying the information it depends on and what triggers each step. This is the beginning of a Power Automate flow.
Each Power Automate flow saved us a little bit of time, but the biggest effect on the blog was how we used that time.
Telling stories to the right people
The most significant thing we’ve noticed since adopting the Sharepoint List and adding automations is that blogs get published much quicker.

Previously, we were so busy with administrative tasks that we didn’t have much time to discuss ideas with the people who suggested them. Complete drafts would land on our doorstep needing significant edits to shape them to the intended audience and objectives. There would be a lot of back and forth between our team, the author and approvers, slowing publication down. Now we can invest lots of time upfront to supporting people in turning their ideas into well-structured, relevant and compelling stories, meaning they are approved more quickly.

Handing the admin tasks over to Power Automate has also improved our ability to multi-task. We can now accept and support more ideas simultaneously, making our team more approachable and useful to the whole directorate.
The biggest benefit we’ve seen isn’t that an approval email now sends itself, it’s that we are spending less time administering content and more time improving it.
Has automation boosted readership?

In short, no. We haven’t seen a significant increase in page views since introducing the automation. However, we are using more of our spare time to tailor the way we share our blog posts to suit the author’s individual objectives. Instead of sharing links with a broad, generic audience, we are targeting niche communities to identify people who will genuinely benefit from it and want to join the conversation.

Now we are seeing more engagement between our audience and our authors, including comments, follow-up messages, and even invitations to speak at events. Importantly, we have a central location to record that engagement and follow up.
The biggest lesson wasn't about automation

You don’t need to run a blog yourself to benefit from what we’ve learned. Whatever team you work in, and whether you consider yourself to be “technical” or not, there is probably a process in your workflow that you could automate.

In our case, trying to automate tasks taught us that the information our tasks depend on needed to be organised. As it turns out, even Comms teams need solid data structures. Organising our data was the most important step in freeing us from cumbersome admin.
There are still more tasks in our workflow that could be automated, and every new automation reveals new ways in which we could improve our data structures.
What process could you automate?

Pick one process that you or your team does repeatedly. Ask yourself what information the process uses, where it lives, what triggers your tasks and which parts of the process require someone to manually find, copy, chase or update something.
You may have found your first automation. More importantly, you know what information to build it on.

description: Automating our blog tasks taught us that the information they depended on needed to be organised. This was the most important step in freeing us from the admin that was slowing us down.

title: Defra launches new research in the Amazon, Congo and Coral Triangle

content.content: This week sees the 17th UN Biodiversity Conference of Parties get underway in Yerevan, Armenia. Minister for Nature Jenny Riddell Carpenter will represent the UK, along with the Special Representative for Nature, Ruth Davis. They will highlight UK leadership on biodiversity, including progress towards 30by30, nature recovery, sustainable development, nature finance, and international partnerships that support global implementation.

This follows last week’s publication of the 2026 Living Planet Report by WWF, which sets out the unprecedented scale and pace at which nature is declining around the world. However, it also offers a message of hope, with examples like the 70% increase in tiger populations in 15 years. I was taken aback a year ago seeing tuna jumping off the south coast of England for the first time in my life. Another example of nature recovery set out in the report.

Around the world the fate of people and ecosystems are intertwined. This is especially true in developing countries, where around a third of jobs are directly dependent on biodiversity. People rely on ecosystems to sustain fisheries, farming (through pollination and soil fertility) and forestry.

Ecosystems also help buffer the world’s rural poor from the worst effects of climate change. For example, through the role of mangroves in protecting coastlines, and forests in regulating local climate, water resources and flooding. Whilst the poorest people in the world are amongst the most exposed to nature loss and climate change, poverty also drives the over exploitation of ecosystems, accelerating its decline.

Recent work by Defra has illustrated the threat to UK national security posed by the degradation or potential collapse of globally important ecosystems such as the Amazon, Congo Basin and Coral Triangle.
Systemic change is required

WWF’s report shows that the majority of biodiversity loss is driven by three human systems: energy, food and finance. It argues that conservation alone will not reverse biodiversity decline without transforming these systems.

The scale of the challenge is huge (the UN Environment Programme estimate that for every $1 spent protecting nature around the world, $30 are spent destroying it). In a world of economic pressures this is a big gap to bridge through traditional development or conservation funding.

The recent Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Transformative Change Assessment shows that reversing biodiversity loss will require transformative change that addresses the underlying causes of environmental decline, rather than focusing solely on its symptoms. It sets out a number of levers to address biodiversity loss at scale, such as by reorganising the sectors driving biodiversity loss, changing economic systems, enhancing governance and engaging with how people use, value and manage nature.
Evidence remains limited on how transformative change happens in practice and under what conditions it can deliver equitable and lasting outcomes for both people and nature.
Defra is calling for new research on transformative change
Through our research programmes, Defra is leading the way in exploring how to apply such systemic approaches to global ecosystem protection.

Through the Global Centre on Biodiversity for Climate programme (known as GCBC), we have launched a new research call on "Enabling transformative change: addressing drivers of biodiversity loss in three critical regions."
This call will fund research to design and test ways to reconfigure the institutions, markets and governance systems that drive biodiversity loss. It focuses on three interconnected areas:

• Socio-ecological dynamics and transformative pathways: how human behaviour, resource use and ecological change interact through feedback loops, and where the leverage points for transformative change can occur.
• Commodity markets and financial flows: the conditions under which supply-chain interventions, regulation and subsidy reform can shift production and investment away from ecosystem degradation.

• Governance and institutions: which governance arrangements – national, regional and transboundary – deliver sustainable biodiversity and livelihood outcomes, including in fragile and conflict-affected settings.
The research will focus on globally important ecosystems
The competition will focus on three globally important regions that are vulnerable to biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation, as highlighted in the UK Nature Security Assessment:

These regions contain some of the world's most important terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems. They support extraordinary biodiversity while also providing essential resources and livelihoods for millions of people.

By funding research across different contexts, GCBC can generate practical evidence on what works, help inform policy and investment decisions, and support the kind of transformational change needed to protect nature and improve outcomes for people.
Turning evidence into action

The new call complements an already powerful portfolio of GCBC research, which is finding new ways to protect poor communities from the impacts of climate change by restoring and harnessing biodiversity. Since its launch, the programme has funded 59 projects across 43 countries in Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia and the Pacific committing around £40 million to biodiversity and climate research around the world.

GCBC-funded research is already showing how evidence can shape real-world decisions. For example, research on multifunctional agroforestry in the Ethiopian highlands has helped translate project insights into national policy on sustainable land use, livelihoods and resilient landscapes. It is a strong example of the kind of practical impact GCBC aims to build on through its next research competition.

Ultimately, the GCBC generates evidence that supports action. We are looking for ambitious, high-quality proposals that can help answer important questions about how societies can better protect, restore and sustainably manage biodiversity.

Successful projects will generate learning, approaches, tools or methodologies that could be scaled up or replicated elsewhere, contributing to a growing evidence base that can inform decisions, shape practical action and support change beyond the places where the research takes place.

Defra will use evidence generated by the research we fund to inform the design of our international aid programmes, interventions in nature finance, and support us in driving an agenda for systemic change through international negotiations.
Find out more and apply
The application window for Concept Notes is now open. Eligible research organisations are encouraged to review the competition materials and consider applying.
Further information on the competition theme, eligibility requirements and application process is available on the GCBC website.

description: In the first of our blog posts on the 17th UN Biodiversity Conference, Dan McGonigle tells us about new research that will help shape practical action for nature.

title: Building resilience and growth in the UK chemical sector

content.content: Chemicals are critical to the UK’s national security, resilience and economy. They underpin essential sectors such as food, healthcare, energy and defence. However, despite its strategic importance, there are substantial pressures facing the UK chemical sector, including high energy costs, ageing infrastructure, and under-investment in innovation. These pressures are compounded by regulatory complexity, policy instability, the absence of a long-term strategy, and fragmented responsibility across government.

In response to these challenges, the Council for Science and Technology (CST) has been advising government this year on the conditions needed to safeguard critical chemical capabilities while supporting innovation and growth. On 25 August, CST published a letter with two specific recommendations:
Recommendation 1: Ministerial accountability for capabilities and innovation

CST’s first recommendation was to appoint a minister with accountability for safeguarding the UK’s critical chemical capabilities and delivering future innovation and empowered to coordinate policy across government, identify the sector’s role in delivering government priorities, and resolve trade-offs between policies and departments.

Government has now appointed a Minister for Reindustrialisation, sitting across the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) with responsibility for chemicals.
Recommendation 2: A roadmap based on national outcomes

CST’s second recommendation was for government to develop a clear, long-term roadmap for the UK chemical sector within 12 months. It should define the national outcomes, capabilities, and supply chains needed for resilience in 2035, then identify the actions, assets, skills, and regulatory conditions required.

The roadmap should guide government, businesses, and investors in deciding which capabilities to retain domestically and where reliable alternatives could meet national needs. It should also address the viability, innovation, investment, and the transition to a competitive, lower-carbon, and more circular industry, supported by proportionate regulation that protects people and the environment.

CST will continue to support government to explore the challenges faced by the chemical sector and solutions to them. This will include through engagement with the wider community at an event co-hosted with the Foundation for Science and Technology (FST) coming December 2026.
Read CST’s full advice on achieving stability and growth in the UK chemical sector and follow the CST blog for future updates.

description: CST sets out how accountable leadership and a long-term roadmap could support a more resilient, innovative, and competitive UK chemical sector.

title: What is ‘AI Sovereignty’?

content.content: AI sovereignty is important because the choices the UK makes now will shape long-term competitiveness, resilience, public trust and strategic autonomy. The Council believes that government needs a clear view of where national capability matters, where dependence is acceptable, and where the UK has a credible opportunity to lead.
For CST, an important first step towards achieving AI sovereignty is defining what it means for the UK in practice.
What is ‘AI Sovereignty’?
While some use ‘AI sovereignty’ to refer to control over AI technologies and models, CST has proposed a broader definition:

With this in mind, achieving AI sovereignty depends on the UK developing the right skills, organisations, data, and technical strengths to deliver the outcomes that the UK wants. In practice, this means deciding where the UK should build its own capability, where it should collaborate with trusted partners, and where resilient access to technology developed elsewhere is sufficient.
The aim of sovereignty is therefore not complete self-sufficiency, but retaining enough agency to shape how AI is developed and used by our services, businesses, and people.1
Achieving AI sovereignty
To help realise this opportunity, CST proposed four recommendations to government:
The full CST advice can be found: AI sovereignty: preserving UK agency in an AI-enabled world - GOV.UK.
CST will continue to engage with ministers and policy makers to support the implementation of recommendations.

description: CST has been advising the UK government on how the UK can achieve AI sovereignty. An important first step is defining what ‘AI sovereignty’ means for the UK.

title: Putting trees to work on your farm
categories: Payments to plant trees and manage woodland

content.content: Whether you're looking to improve productivity, create new income opportunities, protect your land from extreme weather or support nature, trees can play an important role on farms across England.

Many farmers are already planting trees in ways that complement food production, from integrating trees into grazing and arable systems through agroforestry to creating new woodland on less productive areas of land.

There is a wide range of funding, advice and practical guidance to help you get started. In this post, we've brought together the key resources to help you make an informed decision about whether tree planting is right for you and your land, outline available funding, and share guidance on bringing existing woodland into management.
The benefits of trees
Trees can deliver a range of benefits for farm businesses.

They can provide shade and shelter for livestock, helping to reduce heat stress in summer and exposure to cold winds during winter. For arable farms, trees can help reduce wind damage to crops and create conditions that support pollinators and natural pest control.

Trees can also improve soil health, reduce erosion and slow water run-off. This all contributes to improving water quality. Trees provide a natural barrier to prevent farm pollutants from reaching water courses.
Woodland and agroforestry systems can also create opportunities to diversify farm income through timber, woodfuel, environmental markets and grants, recreation and supporting tourism.
Agroforestry: productive farming with trees
Planting trees does not have to mean taking land out of food production.

Agroforestry is the practice of integrating trees with crops and livestock on the same parcel of land. It enables farmers to continue producing food while benefiting from the advantages trees can bring.
Examples include:
Agroforestry can help improve resilience to climate challenges, enhance biodiversity and support long-term farm productivity.

Want to get started with in-field Agroforestry? If you're thinking about introducing agroforestry on your farm, an agroforestry plan can help you decide which approach is right for your land and business and identify the best locations for trees. Funding is available through the PA4: Agroforestry plan capital item to support you in developing your plan.
In July we made it possible for farmers and land managers to access capital items to create in-field agroforestry year-round via the Higher Tier Capital Grants offer.
Once you’ve got an approved agroforestry plan and have the trees planted, you can submit an expression of interest for a Higher Tier application.
The Forestry Commission’s Guide to agroforestry explains the different approaches and includes practical information to help you decide whether it could work for your business.
If you want to understand how you could implement agroforestry on your farm, and put your questions to a panel of experts, the Forestry Commission are leading two webinars in November:
Woodland creation: making marginal land work harder
For many farms, woodland creation can be a way of generating greater value from land that delivers limited agricultural returns.
Areas such as steep slopes, wet fields, awkward corners and less productive parcels may be well suited to tree planting.
Creating woodland can:

Woodland creation does not need to involve large-scale planting. Smaller farm woodlands, shelterbelts, riparian planting and strategic blocks of trees can all contribute to broader farm business objectives.

If you want to explore woodland creation, the ‘Tree planting and woodland creation: overview’ page on GOV.UK explains the process, available support and what to consider before planting. We also touch on some of this in the section below.
Funding available for tree planting
If you're considering planting trees, funding is available through a number of schemes.
Don't know where to start? The Woodland Creation Planning Grant (WCPG) provides funding to prepare a woodland creation design plan.

The main woodland creation grant available in England is the England Woodland Creation Offer (EWCO). EWCO provides payments towards the cost of establishing new broadleaf, conifer and mixed woodland and offers additional contributions where projects deliver wider environmental benefits, including nature recovery, water quality improvements and flood mitigation.

The best place to find up-to-date information on available grants is the ‘Funding for farmers, growers and land managers page on GOV.UK’. This includes information on current farming and forestry funding opportunities and can help you identify the support most relevant to your holding, including regionally targeted grants for woodland creation.
Government tree planting grants offer an average of £19,000 per hectare for planting and establishment – helping cover the costs so you can see the benefits.
EWCO can be particularly attractive for farmers looking to make better use of less productive or difficult-to-farm land.
Bringing existing woodland into management
Many holdings contain woodland that has received little active management for years.

Unlocking the potential of trees and woodland already established on land can bring huge benefits. Bringing these woodlands into management can improve biodiversity, boost land’s ability to cope with climate change, increase resilience to pests and diseases, and create additional income streams.
Active woodland management may include:
Well-managed woodland can become an important long-term asset for a farm business while delivering benefits for nature and the wider environment.

A woodland management plan provides a structured way to plan and organise the management of your woodland to the UK Forestry Standard. Funding is available to support you in developing your plan through the PA3 Woodland Management Plan Capital Grant. Your Forestry Commission Woodland Officer can also give you advice on completing a woodland plan.
A lot of capital item funding, such as the Woodland Management Plan, is currently available year-round, as well as via Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT).
Farmers and land managers interested in managing existing woodland should explore the support and guidance available through CSHT.
Depending on your objectives, Higher Tier can support you to manage valuable native woodland habitat, restore ancient woodland and improve the resilience of your woodland asset.

You can pick and choose funding options to suit the management ambitions outlined on your woodland management plan. You can build on the straightforward woodland improvement actions to support species recovery and management, permissive access, water management and heritage ambitions for your woodland.
You can also access funding to support species recovery and management, permissive access, wetland and heritage ambitions for your woodland.

A combination of capital items and a CSHT agreement can complement each other to reward farmers for effective woodland management. Unlocking unmanaged woodland assets through Higher Tier often requires improving access, which can be done via the Woodland infrastructure capital item.

Annex D of the Higher Tier applicants guide outlines all the funding available to support woodland improvement. A Forestry Commission Woodland Officer will also be able to discuss available funding and items with you, as part of your CSHT application.
There is also separate support available to restock or improve woodland after tree health problems.
Free advice from the Forestry Commission
If you're not sure where to begin, help is available. This support can help you make informed decisions before committing to a project.

The Forestry Commission can provide Woodland Creation Opportunity Reports, giving you tailored information about where woodland creation may be suitable and the opportunities it could create on your holding.
Local expert advisors are on-hand to offer free bespoke guidance to help you through the entire creation process, or to advise on woodland management.
Find out more
Whether you're interested in agroforestry, planting new woodland or making the most of existing woodland, there is support available to help you take the next step.
Farmers can explore options through Defra's Put Down Roots campaign, which brings together guidance, funding information and examples of how trees are already supporting successful farm businesses.
Trees can help farms become more productive, resilient and diversified. With funding, practical guidance and expert advice available, now is a good time to explore how trees could work on your farm.
Lee Pedley of Tawell Farm shows how planting trees can work alongside farming to improve resilience, support livestock and create a lasting legacy for the next generation:

description: Trees can help make farm businesses more productive, resilient and profitable. From agroforestry and woodland creation to managing existing woodland, discover the funding, advice and support available to help you get started.

title: Different perspectives and shared purpose

content.content: Graham Stallwood, Chief Executive of the Planning Inspectorate, reflects on some of the questions currently being asked about appeals, local plans and how we are preparing for the demands ahead.
I recently joined Have We Got Planning News For You for a wide-ranging conversation about the work of the Planning Inspectorate.

We covered everything from appeal timetables and the choice between hearings and inquiries to the changes to written representations and the significant number of local plans we are expecting over the coming months.
They were challenging questions, but important ones.

Planning works best when organisations across the system are open about the pressures they face, listen to different perspectives and work together to find practical solutions. So, I wanted to reflect on some of the issues raised and explain how we're approaching them.
Getting the balance right on appeal timetables
I know there is concern in parts of the sector about the time being taken to schedule some appeal events.
Most events happen within the windows we're aiming for, but there are currently some hearings and inquiries being scheduled later than I would like.
There are several reasons behind that. Sometimes we need an inspector with specialist knowledge. There can also be complex circumstances involving the parties to an appeal.
We're also preparing for an exceptional amount of local plan work. We're expecting the equivalent of around two-and-a-half to three years' worth of local plans to be submitted in December.

We've recruited around 35 additional inspectors to help us meet that challenge. Those colleagues need to be properly trained and given experience of examinations before taking on cases themselves. That has required some of our experienced inspectors to support their development, with a short-term impact on the resource available elsewhere.
It is a challenge, and I don't want to underplay the effect that delays can have on people using our services. But we're building capacity so that we're better placed to meet the demands ahead.
Predictability shouldn't mean inflexibility
Another concern raised with me was whether the drive to decide appeals within predictable timescales can lead to hearing and inquiry dates being imposed too rigidly.

Government is clear about the importance of greater certainty and predictability in the planning system. That's important not only for appellants, but for local authorities, communities and everyone else affected by a proposal.
There will be occasions when there are good reasons to change an event date. Equally, there will be occasions when delaying it isn't justified. We make those judgements carefully and fairly.
We're looking at how we can develop a clearer, more shared understanding with the sector about how those situations should be approached.
There is a role for all of us here. If we want a quicker and more predictable system, the Inspectorate and the organisations and professionals working with us need to help make that possible.
Fairness sits at the heart of what we do
During the discussion, my weekend role as a grassroots football referee cropped up.

There are, perhaps surprisingly, some similarities. Whether you're on a football pitch or working within the planning system, people want to know they've been heard, that the rules have been applied consistently and that decisions have been reached fairly, even when they don't agree with the outcome.

For me, a fair process isn't simply one where everyone receives the same treatment. People's circumstances differ, and sometimes treating people differently is precisely what's needed to achieve fairness.
What matters is whether people can answer some fundamental questions positively:
Was I listened to? Was the decision-making transparent? Was I treated with respect?
Those principles are fundamental to the legitimacy of the Planning Inspectorate.
They matter whether we're considering a planning appeal, examining a local plan or dealing with one of the many other types of casework that come to us.
Choosing the right procedure for an appeal
We also discussed concerns about some cases being dealt with through hearings rather than inquiries.
The starting point for us isn't how large or valuable a development is. It is what an inspector needs to find out to reach their decision.

If the evidence can be properly assessed through written representations, an oral event shouldn't be necessary. Where evidence needs to be explored further, the inspector will consider whether a hearing or inquiry is the appropriate way to do that.
The important thing is matching the complexity of the case, the inspector's experience and the process.
That principle also applies to the new Part 1 written representations process.

Part 1 does not change the criteria for deciding whether an appeal needs a hearing or inquiry. Where an inspector needs a hearing or inquiry to properly test and understand the evidence, that remains available.
Quality is about much more than the outcome
One question I am regularly asked is whether we look at the proportion of appeals individual inspectors allow or dismiss.
We can see that information, but looking at an inspector's performance simply through an allowed or dismissed percentage would be far too simplistic.

Different types of casework can produce very different patterns. Multiple appeals on one site, enforcement cases and other specialist areas can quickly change the proportion of appeals an Inspector allows or dismisses.
What matters is the quality of the decision.
Our quality assurance therefore looks much more deeply at areas such as the reasoning behind decisions, the way issues have been addressed and the clarity and tone of our work.

I don't want inspectors worrying about whether their next decision will increase or decrease an allowance rate. I want them concentrating on making the right decision based on the evidence in front of them in a consistently timely way.
Preparing for what's ahead
The Planning Inspectorate's work extends much further than the planning appeals most people are familiar with.

We deal with more than 40 different types of casework, from planning and enforcement appeals and local plan examinations to nationally significant infrastructure projects, rights of way, compulsory purchase orders and a range of other applications and decisions.
That breadth means we constantly need to think about where our expertise and resources are needed most.
The forthcoming influx of local plans will undoubtedly be a challenge. But we've been preparing for it.

Our new inspectors come from a range of built-environment professions, and they're already gaining experience alongside established inspectors. That's important not only for the immediate challenge but for developing the capability we'll need in the years ahead.
Working together
One thing my career in planning has taught me is that no single organisation or profession can make the planning system work on its own.
Local authorities, applicants, communities, developers, planning professionals, government and the Planning Inspectorate all see the system from slightly different perspectives.

Understanding those perspectives doesn't mean we will always agree. But being curious about them, listening to concerns and being prepared to work across organisational and professional boundaries gives us a much better chance of improving the system.
We want a Planning Inspectorate that makes high-quality decisions, treats people fairly and provides greater certainty about how long processes will take.
Those objectives aren't alternatives.
The challenge for us, and for the wider planning sector, is delivering them together.
Graham Stallwood Chief Executive, Planning Inspectorate

title: Our T Level Success Story

content.content: Happy National T Levels Week! Running from 19 to 23 October, it’s the perfect time to celebrate how these placements are bringing fresh energy to our teams. We are excited to share the Going Forward into Employment (GFIE) team’s recent experiences.
What is T Levels Week?
T Levels Week celebrates T Levels—two-year technical qualifications co-designed with employers to equip young people for skilled careers.
It brings together schools, colleges, employers, and students to highlight the value of technical education and share success stories from across the country.

Speaking of success stories, we have some fantastic news of our own to celebrate: one of our very own GFIE Team members has just been named a Regional Winner for The Outstanding T Level Ambassador of the Year Award 2026!
We are incredibly proud of their dedication to championing technical education and supporting the next generation of talent
What are T Levels?

While awareness is still growing—around 60% to 70% of students, parents, and employers remain unfamiliar with them—T Levels are two-year technical qualifications in England for 16-to-19-year-olds after GCSEs. Equivalent to three A Levels, they blend 80% classroom study with 20% hands-on industry placement, offering a practical path alongside traditional academic or apprenticeship options.
A recent report by Alan Milburn emphasised the importance of connecting schools with employers.
By offering placements across diverse regions and teams, we help ensure work experience is accessible based on drive and capability rather than personal connections.
Get Involved with T Levels
Whether you are looking to kickstart your career, support your child's future, or bring fresh talent into your team, T Levels offer an exciting path forward.
Find out more about how T Levels can work for you, visit GOV.UK T Levels and Amazing Apprenticeships

title: From Research to Recommendation: My Summer in DDaT at UKEF

content.content: Over the last few months, I had an opportunity to intern in the Data, Digital and Technology (DDaT) division in UK Export Finance. I began this role directly after finishing my degree in law, so I was excited to embark on this adventure in the civil service. I was unsure on whether coming from a non-technical background would make me feel wildly out of my depth. I assumed that delivering digital services in the public sector would require a great deal of specialised technical experience, so I was curious to see how the skills I developed throughout university could add value to projects.

From the outset of my internship, I was welcomed into a friendly team that made integrating into a new environment seamless! To settle in, I had many 1-1 meetings which gave me an opportunity to get to know everyone personally and provided an insight into their daily roles. The introductions helped broaden my understanding of DDaT and put to bed any worries I previously had about coming from a non-technical background.
After those first two weeks, I felt a lot more confident in possible future career choices, and excited to get involved in work impacting users across UKEF.
The Digital & Transformation Playbook

The development of the Digital & Transformation playbook was the main project I worked on during my internship. The project aimed to answer one simple question: How can information across DDaT’s professions be organised in a way that make sense to the diverse teams?

Currently, information is spread across multiple resources and internal sites, resulting in disjointed information and confusing access for users. These pain points underpin the rationale behind developing a playbook which was more connected and usable across teams. Before starting this internship, I thought I would be assisting on the sidelines, but I was grateful to be able to take full ownership of this project from research to prototype iteration. I started to feel less like an intern and more like a colleague in the team.
Through the duration of the project I:
Reflections

One of my biggest take aways from this experience was that understanding users is integral to the success of any digital service. When I first learnt about the playbook, I thought that reorganising information would be the challenge, however, through user research methods, I quickly realised that the greatest challenge is understanding how users navigate and understand information.

This insight made me realise that, contrary to my initial assumption, digital departments do involve a great deal of human interaction demonstrating the importance of empathy and understanding in informing service design.

Perhaps my greatest reflection of the internship was that growth and confidence come from being trusted. In my first week I would not have thought that I would be independently leading such a major project, especially in a digital space. From researching to iterating prototypes, I surprised myself with the work I was able to take ownership of.

I wouldn’t have been able to do this without my wonderful team that were so helpful and supportive. I am super grateful for my incredible line manager, Ben Johnson, who gave me the foundation of confidence I needed to achieve such amazing things over the internship. I am immensely thankful for the time and effort that the team so generously offered and following this internship I am excited about the possibility of pursuing a career in the Civil Service.
This experience was truly a once in a lifetime opportunity and I feel ever so privileged to have started the first leg of my career in UKEF.

title: Opening GOV.UK Wallet sandbox to digital verification services
authors: Nicola Betz, Head of Policy, Strategy & Engagement, GOV.UK One Login & GOV.UK Wallet

content.content: The Government Digital Service (GDS) is inviting registered digital verification service (DVS) providers to join the GOV.UK Wallet sandbox. This will be the first time that private sector organisations can test their verifier technology in a closed test environment (the sandbox) with a test digital driving licence.

This is a significant moment in the development of the digital driving licence. It allows us to start testing how services offered by DVS providers will interact with government issued credentials in the GOV.UK Wallet, helping us to learn, improve and build confidence before we start to introduce the digital driving licence from next year.

DVS providers who are independently certified against government standards and are on the government’s DVS register can join the sandbox. The technology they provide will enable information from the digital driving licence to be shared securely with other organisations who will accept the digital driving licence, such as pubs, cinemas and supermarkets.

Our approach helps people use digital credentials with confidence, knowing they are sharing information through trusted providers. This will also help to support the wider use of trusted digital credentials in the future.
Responsible, safe and secure technology
As you would expect for a product that will in time be available to millions of people across the UK, we are building the digital driving licence in a responsible, safe and secure way.
Following on from our testing at the end of last year, GDS and the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) have continued to design, build and test the product. This has included:

We have also been building on the work of the first credential for the GOV.UK Wallet, the digital Veteran Card. Like the Veteran Card, the digital driving licence is designed to be an alternative to the physical card, not a replacement for it.
The sandbox goes live

The sandbox gives registered DVS providers access to a collection of tools, including test credentials and test data, allowing them to experiment and build integrations in a safe environment that is separate from live user data and designed specifically for testing and learning.
Specifically, the sandbox allows DVS providers to:

This collaboration in the test environment enables learning on both sides. DVS providers gain an opportunity to prepare their own services, while government gains valuable insight into how the ecosystem will work in real life.
Working with industry to prepare for rollout
Many organisations will play a role in helping people use and verify digital credentials in the future. DVS providers are a key part of that.

Working closely with DVS providers helps us understand how digital credentials will operate in practice, are shared securely, and identify issues early. That’s why we're creating opportunities for industry partners to test, learn and share feedback as the programme develops.
What’s next
Building and inviting the DVS providers into the sandbox is one step in a wider programme of testing and collaboration.
Later this year, GDS will host a testing event with stakeholders to help us further test technical integration and collect feedback ahead of launch. More information on this will follow.
This work aims to build confidence across the whole system:
Transforming the driver experience

The Roadmap for modern digital government sets out to make life easier for people, drive growth and deliver on smarter, more efficient public services. The digital driving licence is part of this transformation, and is being achieved alongside other important product updates for drivers. This includes the GOV.UK App adding the Driver and vehicles account feature as a native feature, which is now in testing with wider release planned in a few months.
Together, these products will make it easier for people to interact with government in ways that are convenient for them, delivering on the Roadmap’s ambitions.
If you’re a registered DVS provider, register for access to the GOV.UK Wallet sandbox

title: Food Crime Update

content.content: Cymraeg

Trust in food isn’t something we can take for granted and one of the biggest threats to that trust is food crime. Sadly, there will always be individuals who are willing to risk confidence in British food for a quick profit, which is why the on-going work of the FSA’s National Food Crime Unit (NFCU) remains so essential. The past few months have shown just how active this fight continues to be.

In Dudley, a joint operation with the local council and police partners uncovered an unapproved meat cutting plant, leading to four arrests and the removal of more four tonnes of illegal meat from the food chain. In another operation, involving multiple partners including the Greater Manchester and Staffordshire Police, and Stoke-on-Trent City Council, an investigation into illegal frozen food products has resulted in one arrest and the seizure of more than 33 tonnes of suspect stock across more than a hundred businesses.

In Leicester, we worked alongside local authorities and the police to tackle the online sale of illegally prepared ‘smokies’, removing unsafe meat from circulation and making one arrest. Meanwhile, in Essex, our officers investigated suspected counterfeit wine worth more than half a million pounds.

These cases span different regions, products, and criminal methods but they share a common thread. Food crime is never victimless. It puts public health at risk, defrauds the public, and undermines the honest businesses that play by the rules. Left unchecked, food crime erodes the confidence that underpins our entire food system.

Protecting the public means staying one step ahead of those who seek to exploit the system for profit. That’s why we need to stay proactive and continue working closely with the police, local authorities, and other partners.

If you would like to keep updated about the risks from food crime and share best practice on strengthening the industry’s response to it, you can subscribe to the NFCU’s news bulletin.  You can also report food crime to Food Crime Confidential, in full confidence, at gov.uk/food-crime/report or by calling 0800 028 1180.
Katie PettiferChief Executive of FSA

title: Why post-market surveillance is a priority for the MHRA AI Airlock programme

content.content: It is widely recognised that AI technologies have the potential to positively transform healthcare by improving patient outcomes, supporting clinical decision-making and helping health services work more efficiently. However, AI systems can behave differently once they move from controlled testing environments into real-world clinical settings. The data, users, workflows and patient populations they encounter may also change over time, and these changes can affect performance.

Manufacturers of medical devices are required to monitor how their devices perform once they are in use. This is achieved through post-market surveillance (PMS), the ongoing process of collecting and reviewing information about a device's safety, performance and effectiveness throughout its lifetime. PMS helps manufacturers identify emerging issues, understand how devices are performing in real-world settings and take action where needed.

However, the importance of PMS extends beyond regulatory compliance. The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare highlighted that AI regulation should be lifecycle-based, recognising that assurance does not end at market entry but continues throughout deployment and use. The Commission also emphasised that the safe adoption of AI is a system-wide responsibility, requiring manufacturers, healthcare organisations, professionals, regulators and others to play a role in identifying, managing and responding to risks as evidence emerges in real-world settings. Finally, as we move into a world where device performance is increasingly data sensitive and may rapidly change, proactively monitoring for and responding to emerging trends will be an important part of safe and responsible device deployment. This blog looks at what the AI Airlock has learned about applying PMS to AI-enabled medical devices, why practical challenges remain, and how the next phase of the programme will build on this work.
What earlier Airlock work told us

Over the past two years, during the pilot and Phase 2, the AI Airlock has explored PMS across a range of candidate technologies through workshops and engagement with regulatory, clinical and technical stakeholders. This work has helped the programme examine how existing PMS requirements apply to AI-enabled medical devices in practice and identify the areas where further evidence and testing are needed.
Phase 1 – FAMOS and continuous monitoring

The pilot phase first explored this challenge through Newton’s Tree’s FAMOS platform, one of the programme’s first four case studies, which examined whether continuous, near-real-time monitoring could strengthen PMS for AI-enabled medical devices. Building on the case study’s real-world testing across 2 deployment sites, a simulation workshop considered how monitoring could detect changes arising from the model, input data and interactions between users and the device, and how the earlier identification of emerging risks and performance changes might support risk management. The case study also explored monitoring measures related to data quality, performance drift and automation bias. Together, the work highlighted the potential for earlier identification of performance trends that could affect safety, while also raising practical questions about access to suitable real-world data, clinically meaningful thresholds, false alarms, stakeholder responsibilities and the action required when a signal is detected (AI Airlock Sandbox Pilot Programme Report; PMS simulation workshop report).
Phase 2: PMS and predetermined change control plans (PCCPs)

Phase 2 tested these questions further across several AI technologies. The Phase 2 findings, captured in the Programme Report, reinforced a central lesson: point-in-time, pre-market validation alone may not fully reflect how an AI medical device will perform in practice. Real-world performance can be difficult to reproduce or to address entirely or accurately in a controlled setting. That is why post-market monitoring needs to be considered early and prospectively designed as complementary to the device’s pre-market evidence, intended use and lifecycle plans.

Phase 2 also examined the relationship between PMS and predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), which describe planned modifications to software and how those modifications will be assessed, across several AI technologies, including through a dedicated simulation workshop. The work showed that managing change in AI-enabled medical devices requires a joined-up lifecycle approach: pre-market evidence should reflect the intended use, deployment environment and anticipated changes, while PMS should monitor real-world performance and identify changes that may affect safety, performance or the device’s intended purpose. The workshop also explored how manufacturers might assess whether a change is significant and whether it falls within an agreed PCCP or requires further regulatory action. Together, the findings highlighted the importance of defining monitoring measures, decision thresholds and responsibilities early, as well as proactively capturing usage and performance data post-market, while retaining sufficient flexibility to respond to evidence generated once the device is in use (AI Airlock Sandbox Phase 2 Programme Report and Insights from the AI Airlock Simulation Workshop: Post Market Surveillance and Predetermined Change Control Plans).
Why PMS remains a practical challenge

While the principles of PMS remain the same, applying them to AI medical devices can present different challenges compared with more traditional or relatively static devices. Unlike fixed devices, AI systems may be particularly sensitive to changes in input data, the clinical environment and the way people use and rely on the device, creating additional complexity when monitoring real-world performance.

The importance of PMS has also been reinforced by the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, which highlighted the need for stronger post-market assurance, including monitoring and the use of real-world evidence. The Commission recognised the Airlock’s findings that assurance for AI does not end at market entry, but must continue throughout the product lifecycle, with manufacturers, healthcare organisations, professionals, regulators and others all playing a role in the safe deployment and oversight of AI technologies.

Manufacturers may therefore need further support to translate existing PMS requirements into monitoring arrangements that are effective and appropriate for AI. The practical questions include what to monitor, how to set clinically meaningful thresholds, how to identify and investigate drift, how to obtain suitable real-world data, and when a detected change should trigger action.

Continuous or near-real-time monitoring may enable emerging trends to be identified earlier, but may not be appropriate in every case. The approach should be proportionate to the device, its risk and the context in which it is used, with a clear purpose for the data collected and agreed responsibilities for reviewing signals and responding to them.

Further clarity may also be needed on the respective roles of manufacturers, healthcare organisations and other actors. The aim is to provide regulatory confidence without imposing impractical monitoring arrangements or generating large volumes of data that do not support meaningful decisions.
What the next phase will explore

Building on these findings, the Airlock has selected post-market surveillance and lifecycle oversight as the first regulatory focus area for Phase 3, recognising the need for further evidence on how these approaches can be applied effectively and proportionately in practice (AI Airlock Phase 3 application).

To help shape this phase, the Airlock held a series of expert stakeholder workshops over the summer with colleagues contributing regulatory, clinical and technical perspectives. The discussions examined how PMS expectations apply to AI-enabled medical devices, including:
These discussions informed the PMS challenge areas and the questions that applicants are now invited to explore.

Supported by multi-year funding from DHSC, Phase 3 will allow the programme to move beyond annual funding cycles, be more flexible in project design and pursue more ambitious, longer-term testing. Working with innovators and stakeholders, the Airlock will explore and test practical approaches to capturing deployment-context factors more proactively; defining meaningful thresholds and proportionate actions when signals arise; maintaining effective monitoring in remote, at-home or direct-to-consumer settings with varying levels of oversight; and ensuring that the right information on safety, performance and change effectively reaches the right people at the right time.

The aim is not to predetermine a single solution or policy position, but to generate evidence about which approaches work in practice, how they can be tailored to a device, its risk and deployment context, and where existing requirements are sufficient or further guidance, tools or regulatory support may be needed. Taking this approach, the Airlock hopes to identify practical, proportionate methodologies and/or processes that support innovation while protecting patients and the public as AI-enabled medical devices are deployed across the health system.

The Phase 3 call for applications is now open and applications can be submitted on a rolling basis. We welcome proposals from AI-enabled medical device developers and manufacturers, providers of solutions to regulatory challenges, and other stakeholders who can help test practical approaches to PMS and lifecycle oversight. If your organisation could contribute to these challenge areas, find out more and apply through the AI Airlock Phase 3 application page. AI Airlock Phase 3 application - GOV.UK.

title: Historic Court Buildings: The Royal Courts of Justice, from Queen Victoria to the bear pit

content.content: Over 1,000 rooms, three and a half miles of corridors, and the biggest Victorian mosaic floor in Europe.

In this episode, we are joined by Richard from the Royal Courts of Justice Estates Office to explore the history of this iconic building, from its construction in the 1880s to its connections with Queen Victoria, who watched barristers arguing below from a balcony, in an area that became known as the 'bear garden'.
We discuss some of the building's more unusual stories, including a mysterious room number staff have never been able to fully remove, and an accident involving the clock tower.

title: Inside Defra's octopus conference

content.content: Since 2025, fishermen in south-west England have seen a sharp increase in octopus catches. While this has created new opportunities for some, others have raised concerns about impacts on shellfish fisheries. Even where the increase has brought benefits, it has meant adapting to a fishery that has looked very different from the one many fishermen have known for years.

Similar increases have been reported elsewhere in Europe over the past few years, raising questions about what is driving the change and what it could mean for the future. There is still no clear agreement on what is causing the increase in octopus numbers, how long they are here to stay, or how fisheries should respond.
Bringing people together

To explore these issues, Defra hosted a conference on 15 October bringing together fishermen, fisheries managers, international experts, and scientists. The conference provided an opportunity for people with different experiences and expertise to share what they are seeing.
Fishermen spoke about the practical impacts on their businesses and local fisheries – setting out both the opportunities and the consequences.
Scientists shared the latest scientific findings and evidence on the species, highlighted the unknowns, and set out what's planned in terms of data collection and research.

International experts shared lessons from their experiences in managing a similar octopus bloom in Brittany - and we also heard from the Marine Stewardship Council on how MSC certified fisheries in Spain and Australia are managed.
Fisheries managers explained the challenges of making decisions when there is still limited evidence.
Participants also discussed ideas for future management and identified priorities for further research.
Reflections from the conference
What did people tell us?
The clearest message from the day was that the increase in octopus numbers is being experienced differently across fisheries and locations.

For some fishermen, increased catches have created a new opportunity. For others, particularly those working in shellfish fisheries, it has added pressure to already challenging conditions and raised concerns about octopus feeding on shellfish, gear interactions, displacement and future access.
What did we learn?

The discussions also showed how much is still unknown. People were keen to better understand whether the increase in octopus numbers is likely to continue, and what, if any, action should be taken while we continue to learn more.

Hearing directly from fishermen, scientists, fisheries managers and speakers from other countries helped bring different perspectives together. It also showed the value of combining practical experience with scientific evidence.
What happens next?

The conference helped us hear different views and experiences from across the fishing industry and fisheries management. A repeated theme was the need for decisions that are evidence-based, adaptable and fair across fisheries.
We will use what we learned, alongside existing evidence and feedback, to identify where more research is needed and help guide future work on octopus in English waters.
Keep up to date

description: Defra brought fishermen, scientists and fisheries managers together to share evidence, discuss impacts and help shape future work on the octopus fishery.

title: Avoidable requisitions are falling. What’s next?
authors: Andrew Robertson, Head of Customer Policy

content.content: At a glance

In our previous blog, Avoidable requisitions continue to fall as we work together, we thanked customers, industry bodies and HM Land Registry caseworkers for helping to reduce avoidable requisitions. To recap, the number of avoidable requisitions has fallen by at least 40% since 2022, and the rate of avoidable issues per 1,000 applications has almost halved.

That progress matters. It means fewer applications are being delayed by issues that could usually have been prevented before submission, less rework for conveyancers, fewer follow-up queries for customers and a smoother process for everyone involved.

But there is still more to do. Avoidable requisitions continue to account for a significant amount of unnecessary work across the registration process. The next phase is about focusing on the issues that still occur most often and taking practical action to prevent them.
Focus checks where they will have most impact

The infographic above groups the leading avoidable requisitions into broad categories, giving an at-a-glance view of where issues arise most often. Recurring themes include missing or unclear information in forms and plans, missing identity and other supporting evidence, and incorrect fees. These are areas where small improvements in preparation and checking can make the next significant difference.

Broad categories such as “missing information” can hide several different problems. Incomplete application details, an unsigned plan and missing Stamp Duty Land Tax evidence each need a different solution. Looking at the individual reasons for requisitions gives firms a clearer basis for checks, training and quality assurance.
Our next infographic shows the leading 10 avoidable points over 2025. A requisition may contain one or more of these:

One of the most effective ways to reduce avoidable requisitions is to understand where they are happening. Many avoidable requisitions can be reduced through simple, consistent checks before submission. These checks do not need to add unnecessary complexity. They are about making sure the application, supporting evidence and any plans tell the same clear story.
The checklist below addresses the current top 10 avoidable requisition points. You can download a copy from our training hub.
Use your data to target improvement

HM Land Registry currently emails avoidable requisition data to customers every six months. We plan to make this data available through Portal, making it easier for firms to identify recurring issues and focus improvement activity.

Different firms will see different patterns. Reviewing avoidable requisition data over time can show where an internal checklist needs updating, where staff may benefit from training or where an additional quality check would prevent repeat problems. Customers can use HM Land Registry support, training and guidance to target specific issues for maximum effect.
What HM Land Registry will do
Customers’ checks are only part of the picture. We will continue to:
Keep the momentum going

Reducing avoidable requisitions is a shared responsibility. Firms can use their data to focus checks and training on the issues that affect them most. HM Land Registry will continue to improve guidance, data, support and caseworker accuracy.
Every preventable issue removed from the process saves time and helps applications progress more smoothly for conveyancers, their clients and HM Land Registry.

description: Avoidable requisitions are falling, but preventable errors still create additional work and delay. We look at the main issues that remain, what firms can do now and how HM Land Registry is supporting further improvement.
